A Vanishing Conjecture on Differential Operators with Constant Coefficients

Wenhua Zhao
Date: August 24, 2026
Abstract.

In the recent progress [BE1], [Me] and [Z2], the well-known JC (Jacobian conjecture) ([BCW], [E]) has been reduced to a VC (vanishing conjecture) on the Laplace operators and HN (Hessian nilpotent) polynomials (the polynomials whose Hessian matrix are nilpotent). In this paper, we first show that the vanishing conjecture above, hence also the JC, is equivalent to a vanishing conjecture for all 2nd order homogeneous differential operators Λ\Lambda and Λ\Lambda-nilpotent polynomials PP (the polynomials P⁡(z)P(z) satisfying Λm​Pm=0\Lambda^{m}P^{m}=0 for all m≥1m\geq 1). We then transform some results in the literature on the JC, HN polynomials and the VC of the Laplace operators to certain results on Λ\Lambda-nilpotent polynomials and the associated VC for 2nd order homogeneous differential operators Λ\Lambda. This part of the paper can also be read as a short survey on HN polynomials and the associated VC in the more general setting. Finally, we discuss a still-to-be-understood connection of Λ\Lambda-nilpotent polynomials in general with the classical orthogonal polynomials in one or more variables. This connection provides a conceptual understanding for the isotropic properties of homogeneous Λ\Lambda-nilpotent polynomials for 2nd order homogeneous full rank differential operators Λ\Lambda with constant coefficients.

Key words and phrases: 
Differential operators with constant coefficients, Λ\Lambda-nilpotent polynomials, Hessian nilpotent polynomials, classical orthogonal polynomials, the Jacobian conjecture.
2000 Mathematics Subject Classification
14R15, 33C45, 32W99

1. Introduction

Let z=(z1,z2,…,zn,…)z=(z_{1},z_{2},\dots,z_{n},\dots) be a sequence of free commutative variables and D=(D1,D2,…,Dn,…)D=(D_{1},D_{2},\dots,D_{n},\dots) with Di:=∂∂ziD_{i}\!:=\frac{\partial}{\partial z_{i}} (i≥1)(i\geq 1). For any n≥1n\geq 1, denote by 𝒜n{\mathcal{A}}_{n} (resp. 𝒜¯n\bar{{\mathcal{A}}}_{n}) the algebra of polynomials (resp. formal power series) in ziz_{i} (1≤i≤n)(1\leq i\leq n). Furthermore, we denote by 𝒟⁡[𝒜n]{\mathcal{D}}[{\mathcal{A}}_{n}] or 𝒟⁡[n]{\mathcal{D}}[n] (resp. 𝔻⁡[𝒜n]{\mathbb{D}}[{\mathcal{A}}_{n}] or 𝔻⁡[n]{\mathbb{D}}[n]) the algebra of differential operators of the polynomial algebra 𝒜n{\mathcal{A}}_{n} (resp. with constant coefficients). Note that, for any k≥nk\geq n, elements of 𝒟⁡[n]{\mathcal{D}}[n] are also differential operators of 𝒜k{\mathcal{A}}_{k} and 𝒜¯k\bar{{\mathcal{A}}}_{k}. For any d≥0d\geq 0, denote by 𝔻d​[n]{\mathbb{D}}_{d}[n] the set of homogeneous differential operators of order dd with constants coefficients. We let 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} (resp. 𝒜¯{\bar{\mathcal{A}}}) be the union of 𝒜n{\mathcal{A}}_{n} (resp. 𝒜¯n\bar{{\mathcal{A}}}_{n}) (n≥1)(n\geq 1), 𝒟{\mathcal{D}} (resp. 𝔻{\mathbb{D}}) the union of 𝒟⁡[n]{\mathcal{D}}[n] (resp. 𝔻⁡[n]{\mathbb{D}}[n]) (n≥1)(n\geq 1), and, for any d≥1d\geq 1, 𝒟d{\mathcal{D}}_{d} the union of 𝒟d​[n]{\mathcal{D}}_{d}[n] (n≥1)(n\geq 1).

Recall that JC (the Jacobian conjecture) which was first proposed by Keller [Ke] in 1939, claims that, for any polynomial map FF of ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n} with Jacobian j⁡(F)=1j(F)=1, its formal inverse map GG must also be a polynomial map. Despite intense study from mathematicians in more than sixty years, the conjecture is still open even for the case n=2n=2. For more history and known results before 20002000 on JC, see [BCW], [E] and references there.

Based on the remarkable symmetric reduction achieved in [BE1], [Me] and the classical celebrated homogeneous reduction [BCW] and [Y] on JC, the author in [Z2] reduced JC further to the following vanishing conjecture on the Laplace operators Δn:=∑i=1nDi2\Delta_{n}\!:=\sum_{i=1}^{n}D_{i}^{2} of the polynomial algebra 𝒜n{\mathcal{A}}_{n} and HN (Hessian nilpotent) polynomials P⁡(z)∈𝒜nP(z)\in{\mathcal{A}}_{n}, where we say a polynomial or formal power series P⁡(z)∈𝒜¯nP(z)\in\bar{{\mathcal{A}}}_{n} is HN if its Hessian matrix Hes ​(P):=(∂2P∂zi​∂zj)n×n\text{Hes\,}(P)\!:=(\frac{\partial^{2}P}{\partial z_{i}\partial z_{j}})_{n\times n} is nilpotent.

Conjecture 1.1.

For any HN ((homogeneous)) polynomial P⁡(z)∈𝒜nP(z)\in{\mathcal{A}}_{n} ((of degree d=4d=4)), we have Δnm​Pm+1​(z)=0\Delta_{n}^{m}P^{m+1}(z)=0 when m>>0m>>0.

Note that, the following criteria of Hessian nilpotency were also proved in Theorem 4.34.3, [Z2].

Theorem 1.2.

For any P⁡(z)∈𝒜¯nP(z)\in\bar{{\mathcal{A}}}_{n} with o⁡(P⁡(z))≥2o(P(z))\geq 2, the following statements are equivalent.

  1. (1)

    P⁡(z)P(z) is HN.

  2. (2)

    Δm​Pm=0\Delta^{m}P^{m}=0 for any m≥1m\geq 1.

  3. (3)

    Δm​Pm=0\Delta^{m}P^{m}=0 for any 1≤m≤n1\leq m\leq n.

Through the criteria in the proposition above, Conjecture 1.1 can be generalized to other differential operators as follows (see Conjecture 1.4 below).

First let us fix the following notion that will be used throughout the paper.

Definition 1.3.

Let Λ∈𝒟⁡[𝒜n]\Lambda\in{\mathcal{D}}[{\mathcal{A}}_{n}] and P⁡(z)∈𝒜¯nP(z)\in\bar{{\mathcal{A}}}_{n}. We say P⁡(z)P(z) is Λ\Lambda-nilpotent if Λm​Pm=0\Lambda^{m}P^{m}=0 for any m≥1m\geq 1.

Note that, when Λ\Lambda is the Laplace operator Δn\Delta_{n}, by Theorem 1.2, a polynomial or formal power series P⁡(z)∈𝒜nP(z)\in{\mathcal{A}}_{n} is Λ\Lambda-nilpotent iff it is HN.

With the notion above, Conjecture 1.1 has the following natural generalization to differential operators with constant coefficients.

Conjecture 1.4.

For any n≥1n\geq 1 and Λ∈𝔻⁡[n]\Lambda\in{\mathbb{D}}[n], if P⁡(z)∈𝒜nP(z)\in{\mathcal{A}}_{n} is Λ\Lambda-nilpotent, then Λm​Pm+1=0\Lambda^{m}P^{m+1}=0 when m>>0m>>0.

We call the conjecture above the vanishing conjecture for differential operators with constant coefficients and denote it by VC. The special case of VC with P⁡(z)P(z) homogeneous is called the homogeneous vanishing conjecture and denoted by HVC. When the number nn of variables is fixed, VC (resp. HVC) is called (resp. homogeneous) vanishing conjecture in nn variables and denoted by VC​[n]\mbox{\bf VC}[n] (resp. HVC​[n]\mbox{\bf HVC}[n]).

Two remarks on VC are as follows. First, due to a counter-example given by M. de Bondt (see example 2.4), VC does not hold in general for differential operators with non-constant coefficients. Secondly, one may also allow P⁡(z)P(z) in VC to be any Λ\Lambda-nilpotent formal power series. No counter-example to this more general VC is known yet.

In this paper, we first apply certain linear automorphisms and Lefschetz’s principle to show Conjecture 1.1, hence also JC, is equivalent to VC or HVC for all 2nd order homogeneous differential operators Λ∈𝔻2\Lambda\in{\mathbb{D}}_{2} (see Theorem 2.9). We then in Section 3 transform some results on JC, HN polynomials and Conjecture 1.1 obtained in [Wa], [BE2], [BE3], [Z2], [Z3] and [EZ] to certain results on Λ\Lambda-nilpotent (Λ∈𝔻2)(\Lambda\in{\mathbb{D}}_{2}) polynomials and VC for Λ\Lambda. Another purpose of this section is to give a survey on recent study on Conjecture 1.1 and HN polynomials in the more general setting of Λ∈𝔻2\Lambda\in{\mathbb{D}}_{2} and Λ\Lambda-nilpotent polynomials. This is also why some results in the general setting, even though their proofs are straightforward, are also included here.

Even though, due to M. de Bondt’s counter-example (see Example 2.4), VC does not hold for all differential operators with non-constant coefficients, it is still interesting to consider whether or not VC holds for higher order differential operators with constant coefficients; and if it also holds even for certain families of differential operators with non-constant coefficients. For example, when Λ=D𝐚\Lambda=D^{\bf a} with 𝐚∈ℕn{\bf a}\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n} and |𝐚|≥2|{\bf a}|\geq 2, VC​[n]\mbox{\bf VC}[n] for Λ\Lambda is equivalent to a conjecture on Laurent polynomials (see Conjecture 3.21). This conjecture is very similar to a non-trivial theorem (see Theorem 3.20) on Laurent polynomials, which was first conjectured by O. Mathieu [Ma] and later proved by J. Duistermaat and W. van der Kallen [DK].

In general, to consider the questions above, one certainly needs to get better understandings on the Λ\Lambda-nilpotency condition, i.e. Λm​Pm=0\Lambda^{m}P^{m}=0 for any m≥1m\geq 1. One natural way to look at this condition is to consider the sequences of the form {Λm​Pm|m≥1}\{\Lambda^{m}P^{m}\,|\,m\geq 1\} for general differential operators Λ\Lambda and polynomials P⁡(z)∈𝒜P(z)\in{\mathcal{A}}. What special properties do these sequences have so that VC wants them all vanish? Do they play any important roles in other areas of mathematics?

The answer to the first question above is still not clear. The answer to the later seems to be ”No”. It seems that the sequences of the form {Λm​Pm|m≥1}\{\Lambda^{m}P^{m}\,|\,m\geq 1\} do not appear very often in mathematics. But the answer turns out to be “Yes” if one considers the question in the setting of some localizations ℬ\mathcal{B} of 𝒜n{\mathcal{A}}_{n}. Actually, as we will discuss in some detail in subsection 4.1, all classical orthogonal polynomials in one variable have the form {Λm​Pm|m≥1}\{\Lambda^{m}P^{m}\,|\,m\geq 1\} except there one often chooses P⁡(z)P(z) from some localizations ℬ\mathcal{B} of 𝒜n{\mathcal{A}}_{n} and Λ\Lambda a differential operators of ℬ\mathcal{B}. Some classical polynomials in several variables can also be obtained from sequences of the form {Λm​Pm|m≥1}\{\Lambda^{m}P^{m}\,|\,m\geq 1\} by a slightly modified procedure.

Note that, due to their applications in many different areas of mathematics, especially in ODE, PDE, the eigenfunction problems and representation theory, orthogonal polynomials have been under intense study by mathematicians in the last two centuries. For example, in [SHW] published in 19401940, about 20002000 published articles mostly on one-variable orthogonal polynomials have been included. The classical reference for one-variable orthogonal polynomials is [Sz] (see also [AS], [C], [Si]). For multi-variable orthogonal polynomials, see [DX], [Ko] and references there.

It is hard to believe that the connection discussed above between Λ\Lambda-nilpotent polynomials or formal power series and classical orthogonal polynomials is just a coincidence. But a precise understanding of this connection still remains mysterious. What is clear is that, Λ\Lambda-nilpotent polynomials or formal power series and the polynomials or formal power series P⁡(z)∈𝒜¯nP(z)\in\bar{{\mathcal{A}}}_{n} such that the sequence {Λm​Pm|m≥1}\{\Lambda^{m}P^{m}\,|\,m\geq 1\} for some differential operator Λ\Lambda provides a sequence of orthogonal polynomials lie in two opposite extreme sides, since, from the same sequence {Λm​Pm|m≥1}\{\Lambda^{m}P^{m}\,|\,m\geq 1\}, the former provides nothing but zero; while the later provides an orthogonal basis for 𝒜n{\mathcal{A}}_{n}.

Therefore, one naturally expects that Λ\Lambda-nilpotent polynomials P⁡(z)P(z)∈𝒜n\in{\mathcal{A}}_{n} should be isotropic with respect to a certain ℂ\mathbb{C}-bilinear form of 𝒜n{\mathcal{A}}_{n}. It turns out that, as we will show in Theorem 4.10 and Corollary 4.11, it is indeed the case when P⁡(z)P(z) is homogeneous and Λ∈𝔻2​[n]\Lambda\in{\mathbb{D}}_{2}[n] is of full rank. Actually, in this case Λm​Pm+1\Lambda^{m}P^{m+1} (m≥0)(m\geq 0) are all isotropic with respect to same properly defined ℂ\mathbb{C}-bilinear form. Note that, Theorem 4.10 and Corollary 4.11 are just transformations of the isotropic properties of HN nilpotent polynomials, which were first proved in [Z2]. But the proof in [Z2] is very technical and lacks any convincing interpretations. From the “formal” connection of Λ\Lambda-nilpotent polynomials and orthogonal polynomials discussed above, the isotropic properties of homogeneous Λ\Lambda-nilpotent polynomials with Λ∈𝔻2​[n]\Lambda\in{\mathbb{D}}_{2}[n] of full rank become much more natural.

The arrangement of the paper is as follows. In Section 2, we mainly show that Conjecture 1.1, hence also JC, is equivalent to VC or HVC for all Λ∈𝔻2\Lambda\in{\mathbb{D}}_{2} (see Theorem 2.9). One consequence of this equivalence is that, to prove or disprove VC or JC, the Laplace operators are not the only choices, even though they are the best in many situations. Instead, one can choose any sequence Λnk∈𝔻2\Lambda_{n_{k}}\in{\mathbb{D}}_{2} with strictly increasing ranks (see Proposition 2.10). For example, one can choose the “Laplace operators” with respect to the Minkowski metric or symplectic metric, or simply choose Λ\Lambda to be the complex ∂¯\bar{\partial}-Laplace operator Δ∂¯,k\Delta_{\bar{\partial},k} (k≥1)(k\geq 1) in Eq. (2.11)(\ref{cx-Delta}).

In Section 3, we transform some results on JC, HN polynomials and Conjecture 1.1 in the literature to certain results on Λ\Lambda-nilpotent (Λ∈𝔻2)(\Lambda\in{\mathbb{D}}_{2}) polynomials P⁡(z)P(z) and VC for Λ\Lambda. In subsection 3.1, we discuss some results on the polynomial maps and PDEs associated with Λ\Lambda-nilpotent polynomials for Λ∈𝔻2​[n]\Lambda\in{\mathbb{D}}_{2}[n] of full rank (see Theorems 3.1–3.3). The results in this subsection are transformations of those in [Z1] and [Z2] on HN polynomials and their associated symmetric polynomial maps.

In subsection 3.2, we give four criteria of Λ\Lambda-nilpotency (Λ∈𝔻2)(\Lambda\in{\mathbb{D}}_{2}) (see Propositions 3.4, 3.6, 3.7 and 3.10). The criteria in this subsection are transformations of the criteria of Hessian nilpotency derived in [Z2] and [Z3]. In subsection 3.3, we transform some results in [BCW], [Wa] and [Y] on JC; [BE2] and [BE3] on symmetric polynomial maps; [Z2], [Z3] and [EZ] on HN polynomials to certain results on VC for Λ∈𝔻2\Lambda\in{\mathbb{D}}_{2}. Finally, we recall a result in [Z3] which says, VC over fields kk of characteristic p>0p>0, even under some conditions weaker than Λ\Lambda-nilpotency, actually holds for any differential operators Λ\Lambda of k⁡[z]k[z] (see Proposition 3.22 and Corollary 3.23).

In subsection 3.4, we consider VC for high order differential operators with constant coefficients. In particular, we show in Proposition 3.18 VC holds for Λ=δk\Lambda=\delta^{k} (k≥1)(k\geq 1), where δ\delta is a derivation of 𝒜{\mathcal{A}}. In particular, VC holds for any Λ∈𝔻1\Lambda\in{\mathbb{D}}_{1} (see Corollary 3.19). We also show that, when Λ=D𝐚\Lambda=D^{\bf a} with 𝐚∈ℕn{\bf a}\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n} and |𝐚|≥2|{\bf a}|\geq 2, VC is equivalent to a conjecture, Conjecture 3.21, on Laurent polynomials. This conjecture is very similar to a non-trivial theorem (see Theorem 3.20) first conjectured by O. Mathieu [Ma] and later proved by J. Duistermaat and W. van der Kallen [DK].

In subsection 4.1, by using Rodrigues’ formulas Eq. (4.1)(\ref{Rodrigues}), we show that all classical orthogonal polynomials in one variable have the form {Λm​Pm|m≥1}\{\Lambda^{m}P^{m}\,|\,m\geq 1\} for some P⁡(z)P(z) in certain localizations ℬ\mathcal{B} of 𝒜n{\mathcal{A}}_{n} and Λ\Lambda a differential operators of ℬ\mathcal{B}. We also show that some classical polynomials in several variables can also be obtained from sequences of the form {Λm​Pm|m≥1}\{\Lambda^{m}P^{m}\,|\,m\geq 1\} with a slight modification. Some of the most classical orthogonal polynomials in one or more variables are briefly discussed in Examples 4.2–4.5, 4.8 and 4.9. In subsection 4.2, we transform the isotropic properties of homogeneous HN homogeneous polynomials derived in [Z2] to homogeneous Λ\Lambda-nilpotent polynomials for Λ∈𝔻2​[n]\Lambda\in{\mathbb{D}}_{2}[n] of full rank (see Theorem 4.10 and Corollary 4.11).

2. The Vanishing Conjecture for the 2nd Order Homogeneous Differential Operators with Constant Coefficients

In this section, we apply certain linear automorphisms and Lefschetz’s principle to show Conjecture 1.1, hence also JC, is equivalent to VC or HVC for all Λ∈𝔻2\Lambda\in{\mathbb{D}}_{2} (see Theorem 2.9). In subsection 2.1, we fix some notation and recall some lemmas that will be needed throughout this paper. In subsection 2.2, we prove the main results of this section, Theorem 2.9 and Proposition 2.10.

2.2. The Vanishing Conjecture for the 2nd Order Homogeneous Differential Operators with Constant Coefficients

In this subsection, we show that Conjecture 1.1, hence also JC, is actually equivalent to VC or HVC for all 2nd order homogeneous differential operators Λ∈𝔻2\Lambda\in{\mathbb{D}}_{2} (see Theorem 2.9). We also show that the Laplace operators are not the only choices in the study of VC or JC (see Proposition 2.10 and Example 2.11).

First, let us point out that VC fails badly for differential operators with non-constant coefficients. The following counter-example was given by M. de Bondt [B].

Example 2.4.

Let xx be a free variable and Λ=x​d2d​x2\Lambda=x\frac{d^{2}}{dx^{2}}. Let P⁡(x)=xP(x)=x. Then one can check inductively that P⁡(x)P(x) is Λ\Lambda-nilpotent, but Λm​Pm+1≠0\Lambda^{m}P^{m+1}\neq 0 for any m≥1m\geq 1.

Lemma 2.5.

For any Λ∈𝒟⁡[n]\Lambda\in{\mathcal{D}}[n], U∈G​L​(n,ℂ)U\in GL(n,\mathbb{C}), A∈S​M​(n,ℂ)A\in SM(n,\mathbb{C}) and P⁡(z)∈𝒜¯nP(z)\in\bar{{\mathcal{A}}}_{n}, we have

  1. (a)(a)

    P⁡(z)P(z) is Λ\Lambda-nilpotent iff ΦU​(P)\Phi_{U}(P) is ΨU​(Λ)\Psi_{U}(\Lambda)-nilpotent. In particular, P⁡(z)P(z) is ΔA\Delta_{A}-nilpotent iff ΦU​(P)=P⁡(U−1​z)\Phi_{U}(P)=P(U^{-1}z) is ΔU​A​Uτ\Delta_{UAU^{\tau}}-nilpotent.

  2. (b)(b)

    VC​[n]\mbox{\bf VC}[n] (resp.HVC[n])(resp.\,\mbox{\bf HVC}[n]) holds for Λ\Lambda iff it holds for ΨU​(Λ)\Psi_{U}(\Lambda). In particular, VC​[n]\mbox{\bf VC}[n] (resp.HVC[n])(resp.\,\mbox{\bf HVC}[n]) holds for ΔA\Delta_{A} iff it holds for ΔU​A​Uτ\Delta_{UAU^{\tau}}.

Proof:  Note first that, for any m,k≥1m,k\geq 1, we have

ΦU​(Λm​Pk)\displaystyle\Phi_{U}\left(\Lambda^{m}P^{k}\right) =(ΦU​Λm​ΦU−1)​ΦU​Pk\displaystyle=(\Phi_{U}\Lambda^{m}\Phi_{U}^{-1})\,\Phi_{U}P^{k}
=(ΦU​Λ​ΦU−1)m​(ΦU​P)k\displaystyle=(\Phi_{U}\Lambda\Phi_{U}^{-1})^{m}(\Phi_{U}P)^{k}
=[ΨU​(Λ)]m​(ΦU​P)k.\displaystyle=[\Psi_{U}(\Lambda)]^{m}(\Phi_{U}P)^{k}.

When Λ=ΔA\Lambda=\Delta_{A}, by Eq. (2.7)(\ref{L2.1-e2}), we further have

ΦU​(ΔAm​Pk)=ΛU​A​Uτm​(ΦU​P)k.\displaystyle\Phi_{U}\left(\Delta_{A}^{m}P^{k}\right)=\Lambda_{UAU^{\tau}}^{m}(\Phi_{U}P)^{k}.

Since ΦU\Phi_{U} (resp. ΨU\Psi_{U}) is an automorphism of 𝒜¯n\bar{{\mathcal{A}}}_{n} (resp. 𝒟⁡[n]{\mathcal{D}}[n]), it is easy to check directly that both (a)(a) and (b)(b) follow from the equations above.  □\Box

Combining the lemma above with Corollary 2.3, we immediately have the following corollary.

Corollary 2.6.

Suppose HVC​[n]\mbox{\bf HVC}[n] ((resp. VC​[n]\mbox{\bf VC}[n])) holds for a differential operator Λ∈𝔻2​[n]\Lambda\in{\mathbb{D}}_{2}[n] of rank r≥1r\geq 1. Then HVC​[n]\mbox{\bf HVC}[n] ((resp. VC​[n]\mbox{\bf VC}[n])) holds for all differential operators Ξ∈𝔻2​[n]\Xi\in{\mathbb{D}}_{2}[n] of rank rr.

Actually we can derive much more (as follows) from the conditions in the corollary above.

Proposition 2.7.

(a)(a) Suppose HVC​[n]\mbox{\bf HVC}[n] holds for a full rank Λ∈𝔻2∘​[n]\Lambda\in{\mathbb{D}}_{2}^{\circ}[n]. Then, for any k≤nk\leq n, HVC​[k]\mbox{\bf HVC}[k] holds for all full rank Ξ∈𝔻2∘​[k]\Xi\in{\mathbb{D}}_{2}^{\circ}[k].

(b)(b) Suppose VC​[n]\mbox{\bf VC}[n] holds for a full rank Λ∈𝔻2∘​[n]\Lambda\in{\mathbb{D}}_{2}^{\circ}[n]. Then, for any m≥nm\geq n, VC​[m]\mbox{\bf VC}[m] holds for all Ξ∈𝔻2​[m]\Xi\in{\mathbb{D}}_{2}[m] of rank nn.

Proof:  Note first that, the cases k=nk=n in (a)(a) and m=nm=n in (b)(b) follow directly from Corollary 2.6. So we may assume k<nk<n in (a)(a) and m>nm>n in (b)(b). Secondly, by Corollary 2.6, it will be enough to show HVC​[k]\mbox{\bf HVC}[k] (k<n)(k<n) holds for Δk\Delta_{k} for (a)(a) and VC​[m]\mbox{\bf VC}[m] (m>n)(m>n) holds for Δn\Delta_{n} for (b)(b).

(a)(a) Let P∈𝒜kP\in{\mathcal{A}}_{k} a homogeneous Δk\Delta_{k}-nilpotent polynomial. We view Δk\Delta_{k} and PP as elements of 𝔻2​[n]{\mathbb{D}}_{2}[n] and 𝒜n{\mathcal{A}}_{n}, respectively. Since PP does not depend on ziz_{i} (k+1≤i≤n)(k+1\leq i\leq n), for any m,ℓ≥0m,\ell\geq 0, we have

Δkm​Pℓ=Δnm​Pℓ.\displaystyle\Delta_{k}^{m}P^{\ell}=\Delta_{n}^{m}P^{\ell}.

Hence, PP is also Δn\Delta_{n}-nilpotent. Since HVC​[n]\mbox{\bf HVC}[n] holds for Δn\Delta_{n} (as pointed out at the beginning of the proof), we have Δkm​Pm+1=Δnm​Pm+1=0\Delta_{k}^{m}P^{m+1}=\Delta_{n}^{m}P^{m+1}=0 when m>>0m>>0. Therefore, HVC​[k]\mbox{\bf HVC}[k] holds for Δk\Delta_{k}.

(b)(b) Let KK be the rational function field ℂ⁡(zn+1,…,zm)\mathbb{C}(z_{n+1},\dots,z_{m}). We view 𝒜m{\mathcal{A}}_{m} as a subalgebra of the polynomial algebra K⁡[z1,…,zn]K[z_{1},\dots,z_{n}] in the standard way. Note that the differential operator Δn=∑i=1nDi2\Delta_{n}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}D_{i}^{2} of 𝒜m{\mathcal{A}}_{m} extends canonically to a differential operator of K⁡[z1,…,zn]K[z_{1},\dots,z_{n}] with constant coefficients.

Since VC​[n]\mbox{\bf VC}[n] holds for Δn\Delta_{n} over the complex field (as pointed out at the beginning of the proof), by Lefschetz’s principle, we know that VC​[n]\mbox{\bf VC}[n] also holds for Δn\Delta_{n} over the field KK. Therefore, for any Δn\Delta_{n}-nilpotent P⁡(z)∈𝒜mP(z)\in{\mathcal{A}}_{m}, by viewing Δn\Delta_{n} as an element of 𝔻2​(K⁡[z1,…,zn]){\mathbb{D}}_{2}(K[z_{1},\dots,z_{n}]) and P⁡(z)P(z) an element of K⁡[z1,…,zn]K[z_{1},\dots,z_{n}] (which is still Δn\Delta_{n}-nilpotent in the new setting), we have Δnk​Pk+1=0\Delta_{n}^{k}P^{k+1}=0 when k>>0k>>0. Hence VC​[m]\mbox{\bf VC}[m] holds for P⁡(z)∈𝒜mP(z)\in{\mathcal{A}}_{m} and Δn∈𝔻2​[m]\Delta_{n}\in{\mathbb{D}}_{2}[m].  □\Box

Proposition 2.8.

Suppose HVC​[n]\mbox{\bf HVC}[n] holds for a differential operator Λ∈𝔻2​[n]\Lambda\in{\mathbb{D}}_{2}[n] with rank r<nr<n. Then, for any k≥rk\geq r, VC​[k]\mbox{\bf VC}[k] holds for all Ξ∈𝔻2​[k]\Xi\in{\mathbb{D}}_{2}[k] of rank rr.

Proof:  First, by Corollary 2.6, we know HVC​[n]\mbox{\bf HVC}[n] holds for Δr\Delta_{r}. To show Proposition 2.8, by Proposition 2.7, (b)(b), it will be enough to show that VC​[r]\mbox{\bf VC}[r] holds for Δr\Delta_{r}.

Let P∈𝒜r⊂𝒜nP\in{\mathcal{A}}_{r}\subset{\mathcal{A}}_{n} be a Δr\Delta_{r}-nilpotent polynomial. If PP is homogeneous, there is nothing to prove since, as pointed out above, HVC​[n]\mbox{\bf HVC}[n] holds for Δr\Delta_{r}. Otherwise, we homogenize P⁡(z)P(z) to P~∈𝒜r+1⊆𝒜n\widetilde{P}\in{\mathcal{A}}_{r+1}\subseteq{\mathcal{A}}_{n}. Since Δr\Delta_{r} is a homogeneous differential operator, it is easy to see that, for any m,k≥1m,k\geq 1, Δrm​Pk=0\Delta_{r}^{m}P^{k}=0 iff Δrm​P~k=0\Delta_{r}^{m}\widetilde{P}^{k}=0. Therefore, P~∈𝒜n\widetilde{P}\in{\mathcal{A}}_{n} is also Δr\Delta_{r}-nilpotent when we view Δr\Delta_{r} as a differential operator of 𝒜n{\mathcal{A}}_{n}. Since HVC​[n]\mbox{\bf HVC}[n] holds for Δr\Delta_{r}, we have that Δrm​P~m+1=0\Delta_{r}^{m}\widetilde{P}^{m+1}=0 when m>>0m>>0. Then, by the observation above again, we also have Δrm​Pm+1=0\Delta_{r}^{m}P^{m+1}=0 when m>>0m>>0. Therefore, VC​[r]\mbox{\bf VC}[r] holds for Δr\Delta_{r}.  □\Box

Now we are ready to prove our main result of this section.

Theorem 2.9.

The following statements are equivalent to each other.

  1. (1)

    JC holds.

  2. (2)

    HVC​[n]\mbox{\bf HVC}[n] (n≥1)(n\geq 1) hold for the Laplace operator Δn\Delta_{n}.

  3. (3)

    VC​[n]\mbox{\bf VC}[n] (n≥1)(n\geq 1) hold for the Laplace operator Δn\Delta_{n}.

  4. (4)

    HVC​[n]\mbox{\bf HVC}[n] (n≥1)(n\geq 1) hold for all Λ∈𝔻2​[n]\Lambda\in{\mathbb{D}}_{2}[n].

  5. (5)

    VC​[n]\mbox{\bf VC}[n] (n≥1)(n\geq 1) hold for all Λ∈𝔻2​[n]\Lambda\in{\mathbb{D}}_{2}[n].

Proof:  First, the equivalences of (1)(1), (2)(2) and (3)(3) have been established in Theorem 7.27.2 in [Z2]. While (4)⇒(2)(4)\Rightarrow(2), (5)⇒(3)(5)\Rightarrow(3) and (5)⇒(4)(5)\Rightarrow(4) are trivial. Therefore, it will be enough to show (3)⇒(5)(3)\Rightarrow(5).

To show (3)⇒(5)(3)\Rightarrow(5), we fix any n≥1n\geq 1. By Corollary 2.6, it will be enough to show VC​[n]\mbox{\bf VC}[n] holds for Δr\Delta_{r} (1≤r≤n)(1\leq r\leq n). But under the assumption of (3)(3) (with n=rn=r), we know that VC​[r]\mbox{\bf VC}[r] holds for Δr\Delta_{r}. Then, by Proposition 2.7, (b)(b), we know VC​[n]\mbox{\bf VC}[n] also holds for Δr\Delta_{r}.  □\Box

Next, we show that, to study HVC, equivalently VC or JC, the Laplace operators are not the only choices, even though they are the best in many situations.

Proposition 2.10.

Let {nk|k≥1}\{n_{k}\,|\,k\geq 1\} be a strictly increasing sequence of positive integers and {Λnk|k≥1}\{\Lambda_{n_{k}}\,|\,k\geq 1\} a sequence of differential operators in 𝔻2{\mathbb{D}}_{2} with rank ​(Λnk)=nk\mbox{rank\,}(\Lambda_{n_{k}})=n_{k} (k≥1)(k\geq 1). Suppose that, for any k≥1k\geq 1, HVC​[Nk]\mbox{\bf HVC}[N_{k}] holds for Λnk\Lambda_{n_{k}} for some Nk≥nkN_{k}\geq n_{k}. Then, the equivalent statements in Theorem 2.9 hold.

Proof:  We show, under the assumption in the proposition, the statement (2)(2) in Theorem 2.9 holds, i.e. for any n≥1n\geq 1, HVC​[n]\mbox{\bf HVC}[n] (n≥1)(n\geq 1) holds for the Laplace operator Δn∈𝔻2​[n]\Delta_{n}\in{\mathbb{D}}_{2}[n].

For any fixed n≥1n\geq 1, let k≥1k\geq 1 such that nk≥nn_{k}\geq n. If Nk=nkN_{k}=n_{k}, then, by Proposition 2.7, (a)(a), we have HVC​[n]\mbox{\bf HVC}[n] (n≥1)(n\geq 1) holds for the Laplace operator Δn∈𝔻2​[n]\Delta_{n}\in{\mathbb{D}}_{2}[n]. If Nk>nkN_{k}>n_{k}, then, by Proposition 2.8, we know VC​[nk]\mbox{\bf VC}[n_{k}] (hence also HVC​[nk]\mbox{\bf HVC}[n_{k}]) holds for Δnk\Delta_{n_{k}}. Since nk≥nn_{k}\geq n, by Proposition 2.7, (a)(a) again, we know HVC​[n]\mbox{\bf HVC}[n] does hold for the Laplace operator Δn\Delta_{n}.  □\Box

Example 2.11.

Besides the Laplace operators, by Proposition 2.10, the following sequences of differential operators are also among the most natural choices.

  1. (1)

    Let nk=kn_{k}=k (k≥2)(k\geq 2) ((or any other strictly increasing sequence of positive integers)). Let Λnk\Lambda_{n_{k}} be the “Laplace operator” with respect to the standard Minkowski metric of ℝnk{\mathbb{R}}^{n_{k}}. Namely, choose

Then, for any k≥1k\geq 1, we set

    More generally, we may also choose Λk=ΔAnk\Lambda_{k}=\Delta_{A_{n_{k}}}, where nk∈ℕn_{k}\in{\mathbb{N}} and Ank∈S​M​(nk,ℂ)A_{n_{k}}\in SM(n_{k},\mathbb{C}) ((not necessarily invertible)) (k≥1)(k\geq 1) with strictly increasing ranks.

3. Some Properties of ΔA\Delta_{A}-Nilpotent Polynomials

As pointed earlier in Section 1 (see page 1), for the Laplace operators Δn\Delta_{n} (n≥1)(n\geq 1), the notion Δn\Delta_{n}-nilpotency coincides with the notion of Hessian nilpotency. HN (Hessian nilpotent) polynomials or formal power series, their associated symmetric polynomial maps and Conjecture 1.1 have been studied in [BE2], [BE3], [Z1]–[Z3] and [EZ]. In this section, we apply Corollary 2.3, Lemma 2.5 and also Lefschetz’s principle to transform some results obtained in the references above to certain results on Λ\Lambda-nilpotent (Λ∈𝔻2)(\Lambda\in{\mathbb{D}}_{2}) polynomials or formal power series, VC for Λ\Lambda and also associated polynomial maps. Another purpose of this section is to give a short survey on some results on HN polynomials and Conjecture 1.1 in the more general setting of Λ\Lambda-nilpotent polynomials and VC for differential operators Λ∈𝔻2\Lambda\in{\mathbb{D}}_{2}.

In subsection 3.1, we transform some results in [Z1] and [Z2] to the setting of Λ\Lambda-nilpotent polynomials for Λ∈𝔻2​[n]\Lambda\in{\mathbb{D}}_{2}[n] of full rank (see Theorems 3.1–3.3). In subsection 3.2, we derive four criteria for Λ\Lambda-nilpotency (Λ∈𝔻2)(\Lambda\in{\mathbb{D}}_{2}) (see Propositions 3.4, 3.6, 3.7 and 3.10). The criteria in this subsection are transformations of the criteria of Hessian nilpotency derived in [Z2] and [Z3].

In subsection 3.3, we transform some results in [BCW], [Wa] and [Y] on JC; [BE2] and [BE3] on symmetric polynomial maps; [Z2], [Z3] and [EZ] on HN polynomials to certain results on VC for Λ∈𝔻2\Lambda\in{\mathbb{D}}_{2}. In subsection 3.4, we consider VC for high order differential operators with constant coefficients. We mainly focus on the differential operators Λ=D𝐚\Lambda=D^{\bf a} (𝐚∈ℕn)({\bf a}\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}). Surprisingly, VC for these operators is equivalent to a conjecture (see Conjecture 3.21) on Laurent polynomials, which is similar to a non-trivial theorem (see Theorem 3.20) first conjectured by O. Mathieu [Ma] and later proved by J. Duistermaat and W. van der Kallen [DK].

3.1. Associated Polynomial Maps and PDEs

Once and for all in this section, we fix any n≥1n\geq 1 and A∈S​M​(n,ℂ)A\in SM(n,\mathbb{C}) of rank 1≤r≤n1\leq r\leq n. We define a ℂ\mathbb{C}-bilinear form ⟨⋅,⋅⟩A\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{A} by setting ⟨u,v⟩A:=uτ​A​v\langle u,v\rangle_{A}\!:=u^{\tau}Av for any u,v∈ℂnu,v\in\mathbb{C}^{n}. By Lemma 2.2, we may write AA as in Eq. (2.8)(\ref{I-r-e}). For any P⁡(z)∈𝒜n¯P(z)\in\bar{{\mathcal{A}}_{n}}, we set

3.2. Some Criteria of ΔA\Delta_{A}-Nilpotency

In this subsection, with the notation and remarks fixed in the previous subsection in mind, we apply the linear automorphism ΦU\Phi_{U} to transform some criteria of Hessian nilpotency derived in [Z2] and [Z3] to criteria of ΔA\Delta_{A}-nilpotency (A∈S​M​(n,ℂ))(A\in SM(n,\mathbb{C})) (see Proposition 3.4, 3.6, 3.7 and 3.10 below).

Proposition 3.4.

Let AA be given as in Eq. (2.8)(\ref{I-r-e}). Then, for any P⁡(z)∈𝒜nP(z)\in{\mathcal{A}}_{n}, it is ΔA\Delta_{A}-nilpotent iff the submatrix of Uτ​(Hes ​P)​UU^{\tau}(\text{Hes\,}P)\,U consisting of the first rr rows and rr columns is nilpotent.

In particular, when r=nr=n, i.e. ΔA\Delta_{A} is full rank, any P​(z)∈𝔻2​[n]P(z)\in{\mathbb{D}}_{2}[n] is ΔA\Delta_{A}-nilpotent iff Uτ​(Hes ​P)​UU^{\tau}(\text{Hes\,}P)\,U is nilpotent.

Proof:  Let P~​(z)\widetilde{P}(z) be as in Eq. (3.1)(\ref{wdP}). Then, as pointed earlier, P⁡(z)P(z) is ΔA\Delta_{A}-nilpotent iff P~​(z)\widetilde{P}(z) is Δr\Delta_{r}-nilpotent.

If r=nr=n, then by Theorem 1.2 , P~​(z)\widetilde{P}(z) is Δr\Delta_{r}-nilpotent iff Hes ​P~​(z)\text{Hes\,}\widetilde{P}(z) is nilpotent. But note that in general we have

(3.16) Hes ​P~​(z)=Hes ​P​(U​z)=Uτ​[(Hes ​P)​(U​z)]​U.\displaystyle\text{Hes\,}\widetilde{P}(z)=\text{Hes\,}P(Uz)=U^{\tau}[(\text{Hes\,}P)(Uz)]\,U.

Assume r<nr<n. We view 𝒜r{\mathcal{A}}_{r} as a subalgebra of the polynomial algebra K⁡[z1,…,zr]K[z_{1},\dots,z_{r}], where KK is the rational field ℂ⁡(zr+1,…,zn)\mathbb{C}(z_{r+1},\dots,z_{n}). By Theorem 1.2 and Lefschetz’s principle, we know that P~\widetilde{P} is Δr\Delta_{r}-nilpotent iff the matrix (∂2P~∂zi​∂zj)1≤i,j≤r\left(\frac{\partial^{2}\widetilde{P}}{\partial z_{i}\partial z_{j}}\right)_{1\leq i,j\leq r} is nilpotent.

Replacing zz by U−1​zU^{-1}z in the submatrix above, we see (∂2P~∂zi​∂zj)1≤i,j≤r\left(\frac{\partial^{2}\widetilde{P}}{\partial z_{i}\partial z_{j}}\right)_{1\leq i,j\leq r} is nilpotent iff the submatrix of Uτ​[Hes ​P​(z)]​UU^{\tau}[\text{Hes\,}P(z)]\,U consisting of the first rr rows and rr columns is nilpotent. Hence the proposition follows.  □\Box

Note that, for any homogeneous quadratic polynomial P⁡(z)=zτ​B​zP(z)=z^{\tau}Bz with B∈S​M​(n,ℂ)B\in SM(n,\mathbb{C}), we have Hes ​P​(z)=2​B\text{Hes\,}P(z)=2B. Then, by Proposition 3.4, we immediately have the following corollary.

Since r≤nr\leq n. We view 𝒜r{\mathcal{A}}_{r} as a subalgebra of the polynomial algebra K⁡[z1,…,zr]K[z_{1},\dots,z_{r}], where KK is the rational field ℂ⁡(zr+1,…,zn)\mathbb{C}(z_{r+1},\dots,z_{n}). 3.3. Some Results on the Vanishing Conjecture of the 2nd Order Homogeneous Differential Operators with Constants Coefficients

In this subsection, we transform some known results of VC for the Laplace operators Δn\Delta_{n} (n≥1)(n\geq 1) to certain results on VC for ΔA\Delta_{A} (A∈S​G​L​(n,ℂ))(A\in SGL(n,\mathbb{C})).

First, by Wang’s theorem [Wa], we know that JC holds for any polynomial maps F⁡(z)F(z) with deg⁡F≤2\deg F\leq 2. Hence, JC also holds for symmetric polynomials F​(z)=z−∇P​(z)F(z)=z-\nabla P(z) with P⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[z]P(z)\in\mathbb{C}[z] of degree d≤3d\leq 3. By the equivalence of JC and VC for the Laplace operators established in [Z2], we know VC holds if Λ=Δn\Lambda=\Delta_{n} and P⁡(z)P(z) is a HN polynomials of degree d≤3d\leq 3. Then, applying the linear automorphism ΦU\Phi_{U}, we have the following proposition.

Theorem 3.12.

For any A∈S​G​L​(n,ℂ)A\in SGL(n,\mathbb{C}) and ΔA\Delta_{A}-nilpotent P⁡(z)∈𝒜nP(z)\in{\mathcal{A}}_{n} ((not necessarily homogeneous)) of degree d≤3d\leq 3, we have Λm​Pm+1=0\Lambda^{m}P^{m+1}=0 when m>>0m>>0, i.e. VC​[n]\mbox{\bf VC}[n] holds for Λ\Lambda and P⁡(z)P(z).

Applying the classical homogeneous reduction on JC (see [BCW], [Y]) to associated symmetric maps, we know that, to show VC for Δn\Delta_{n} (n≥1)(n\geq 1), it will be enough to consider only homogeneous HN polynomials of degree 44. Therefore, by applying the linear automorphism ΦU\Phi_{U} of 𝒜n{\mathcal{A}}_{n}, we have the same reduction for HVC too.

Theorem 3.13.

To study HVC in general, it will be enough to consider only homogeneous P⁡(z)∈𝒜P(z)\in{\mathcal{A}} of degree 44.

In [BE2] and [BE3] it has been shown that JC holds for symmetric maps F​(z)=z−∇P​(z)F(z)=z-\nabla P(z) (P⁡(z)∈𝒜n)(P(z)\in{\mathcal{A}}_{n}) if the number of variables nn is less or equal to 44, or n=5n=5 and P⁡(z)P(z) is homogeneous. By the equivalence of JC for symmetric polynomial maps and VC for the Laplace operators established in [Z2], and Proposition 2.8 and Corollary 2.6, we have the following results on VC and HVC.

Theorem 3.14.

(a)(a) For any n≥1n\geq 1, VC​[n]\mbox{\bf VC}[n] holds for any Λ∈𝔻2\Lambda\in{\mathbb{D}}_{2} of rank 1≤r≤41\leq r\leq 4.

(b)(b) HVC​[5]\mbox{\bf HVC}[5] holds for any Λ∈𝔻2​[5]\Lambda\in{\mathbb{D}}_{2}[5].

Note that the following vanishing properties of HN formal power series have been proved in Theorem 6.26.2 in [Z2] for the Laplace operators Δn\Delta_{n} (n≥1)(n\geq 1). By applying the linear automorphism ΦU\Phi_{U}, one can show it also holds for any Λ\Lambda-nilpotent (Λ∈𝔻2)(\Lambda\in{\mathbb{D}}_{2}) formal power series.

Theorem 3.15.

Let Λ∈𝔻2​[n]\Lambda\in{\mathbb{D}}_{2}[n] and P⁡(z)∈𝒜¯nP(z)\in\bar{{\mathcal{A}}}_{n} be Λ\Lambda-nilpotent with o⁡(P)≥2o(P)\geq 2. The following statements are equivalent.

  1. (1)

    Λm​Pm+1=0\Lambda^{m}P^{m+1}=0 when m>>0m>>0.

  2. (2)

    There exists k0≥1k_{0}\geq 1 such that Λm​Pm+k0=0\Lambda^{m}P^{m+k_{0}}=0 when m>>0m>>0.

  3. (3)

    For any fixed k≥1k\geq 1, Λm​Pm+k=0\Lambda^{m}P^{m+k}=0 when m>>0m>>0.

By applying the linear automorphism ΦU\Phi_{U}, one can transform Theorem 1.51.5 in [EZ] on VC of the Laplace operators to the following result on VC of Λ∈𝔻2\Lambda\in{\mathbb{D}}_{2}.

Theorem 3.16.

Let Λ∈𝔻2​[n]\Lambda\in{\mathbb{D}}_{2}[n] and P⁡(z)∈𝒜¯nP(z)\in\bar{{\mathcal{A}}}_{n} any Λ\Lambda-nilpotent polynomial with o⁡(P)≥2o(P)\geq 2. Then VC holds for Λ\Lambda and P⁡(z)P(z) iff, for any g⁡(z)∈𝒜ng(z)\in{\mathcal{A}}_{n}, we have Λm​(g⁡(z)​Pm)=0\Lambda^{m}(g(z)P^{m})=0 when m>>0m>>0.

In [EZ], the following theorem has also been proved for Λ=Δn\Lambda=\Delta_{n}. Next we show it is also true in general.

Theorem 3.17.

Let A∈S​G​L​(n,ℂ)A\in SGL(n,\mathbb{C}) and P⁡(z)∈𝒜nP(z)\in{\mathcal{A}}_{n} a homogeneous ΔA\Delta_{A}-nilpotent polynomial with deg⁡P≥2\deg P\geq 2. Assume that σA−1​(z):=zτ​A−1​z\sigma_{A^{-1}}(z)\!:=z^{\tau}A^{-1}z and the partial derivatives ∂P∂zi\frac{\partial P}{\partial z_{i}} (1≤i≤n)(1\leq i\leq n) have no non-zero common zeros. Then HVC​[n]\mbox{\bf HVC}[n] holds for ΔA\Delta_{A} and P⁡(z)P(z).

In particular, if the projective subvariety determined by the ideal ⟨P⁡(z)⟩\langle P(z)\rangle of 𝒜n{\mathcal{A}}_{n} is regular, HVC​[n]\mbox{\bf HVC}[n] holds for ΔA\Delta_{A} and P⁡(z)P(z).

Proof:  Let P~\widetilde{P} as given in Eq. (3.1)(\ref{wdP}). By Theorem 1.21.2 in [EZ], we know that, when σ2​(z):=∑i=1nzi2\sigma_{2}(z)\!:=\sum_{i=1}^{n}z_{i}^{2} and the partial derivatives ∂P~∂zi\frac{\partial\widetilde{P}}{\partial z_{i}} (1≤i≤n)(1\leq i\leq n) have no non-zero common zeros, HVC​[n]\mbox{\bf HVC}[n] holds for Δn\Delta_{n} and P~\widetilde{P}. Then, by Lemma 2.5, (b)(b), HVC​[n]\mbox{\bf HVC}[n] also holds for ΔA\Delta_{A} and PP.

But, on the other hand, since UU is invertible and, for any 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n,

∂P~∂zi=∑j=1nuj​i​∂P∂zj​(U​z),\frac{\partial\widetilde{P}}{\partial z_{i}}=\sum_{j=1}^{n}u_{ji}\frac{\partial P}{\partial z_{j}}(Uz),

σ2​(z)\sigma_{2}(z) and ∂P~∂zi\frac{\partial\widetilde{P}}{\partial z_{i}} (1≤i≤n)(1\leq i\leq n) have no non-zero common zeros iff σ2​(z)\sigma_{2}(z) and ∂P∂zi​(U​z)\frac{\partial P}{\partial z_{i}}(Uz) (1≤i≤n)(1\leq i\leq n) have no non-zero common zeros, and iff, with zz replaced by U−1​zU^{-1}z, σ2​(U−1​z)=σA−1​(z)\sigma_{2}(U^{-1}z)=\sigma_{A^{-1}}(z) and ∂P∂zi​(z)\frac{\partial P}{\partial z_{i}}(z) (1≤i≤n)(1\leq i\leq n) have no non-zero common zeros. Therefore, the theorem holds.  □\Box

3.4. The Vanishing Conjecture for Higher Order Differential Operators with Constant Coefficients

Even though the most interesting case of VC is for Λ∈𝔻2\Lambda\in{\mathbb{D}}_{2}, at least when JC is concerned, the case of VC for higher order differential operators with constant coefficients is also interesting and non-trivial. In this subsection, we mainly discuss VC for the differential operators D𝐚D^{\bf a} (𝐚∈ℕn)({\bf a}\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}). At the end of this subsection, we also recall a result proved in [Z3] which says that, when the base field has characteristic p>0p>0, VC, even under a weaker condition, actually holds for any differential operator Λ\Lambda (not necessarily with constant coefficients).

Let βj∈ℂn\beta_{j}\in\mathbb{C}^{n} (1≤j≤ℓ)(1\leq j\leq\ell) be linearly independent and set δj:=⟨βj,D⟩\delta_{j}\!:=\langle\beta_{j},D\rangle. Let Λ=∏j=1ℓδjai\Lambda=\prod_{j=1}^{\ell}\delta_{j}^{a_{i}} with aj≥1a_{j}\geq 1 (1≤j≤ℓ)(1\leq j\leq\ell).

When ℓ=1\ell=1, VC for Λ\Lambda can be proved easily as follows.

Proposition 3.18.

Let δ∈𝔻1​[z]\delta\in{\mathbb{D}}_{1}[z] and Λ=δk\Lambda=\delta^{k} for some k≥1k\geq 1. Then

  1. (a)(a)

    A polynomial P⁡(z)P(z) is Λ\Lambda-nilpotent if ((and only if)) Λ​P=0\Lambda P=0.

  2. (b)(b)

    VC holds for Λ\Lambda.

Proof:  Applying a change of variables, if necessary, we may assume δ=D1\delta=D_{1} and Λ=D1k\Lambda=D_{1}^{k}.

Let P⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[z]P(z)\in\mathbb{C}[z] such that Λ​P​(z)=D1k​P​(z)=0\Lambda P(z)=D_{1}^{k}P(z)=0. Let dd be the degree of P⁡(z)P(z) in z1z_{1}. From the equation above, we have k>dk>d. Therefore, for any m≥1m\geq 1, we have k​m>d​mkm>dm which implies Λm​P​(z)m=D1k​m​Pm​(z)=0\Lambda^{m}P(z)^{m}=D_{1}^{km}P^{m}(z)=0. Hence, we have (a)(a).

To show (b)(b), let P⁡(z)P(z) be a Λ\Lambda-nilpotent polynomial. By the same notation and argument above, we have k>dk>d. Choose a positive integer N>dk−dN>\frac{d}{k-d}. Then, for any m≥Nm\geq N, we have m>dk−dm>\frac{d}{k-d}, which is equivalent to (m+1)​d<k​m(m+1)d<km. Hence we have Λm​P​(z)m+1=D1k​m​Pm+1​(z)=0\Lambda^{m}P(z)^{m+1}=D_{1}^{km}P^{m+1}(z)=0.  □\Box

In particular, when k=1k=1 in the proposition above, we have the following corollary.

Corollary 3.19.

VC holds for any differential operator Λ∈𝔻1\Lambda\in{\mathbb{D}}_{1}.

Next we consider the case ℓ≥2\ell\geq 2. Note that, when ℓ=2\ell=2 and a1=a2=1a_{1}=a_{2}=1. Λ∈𝔻2\Lambda\in{\mathbb{D}}_{2} and has rank 22. Then, by Theorem 3.14, we know VC holds for Λ\Lambda.

Besides the case above, VC for Λ=∏j=1ℓδjai\Lambda=\prod_{j=1}^{\ell}\delta_{j}^{a_{i}} with ℓ≥2\ell\geq 2 seems to be non-trivial at all. Actually, we will show below, it is equivalent to a conjecture (see Conjecture 3.21) on Laurent polynomials.

First, by applying a change of variables, if necessary, we may (and will) assume Λ=D𝐚\Lambda=D^{\bf a} with 𝐚∈(ℕ+)ℓ{\bf a}\in({\mathbb{N}}^{+})^{\ell}. Secondly, note that, for any 𝐛∈ℕn{\bf b}\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n} and h⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[z]h(z)\in\mathbb{C}[z], D𝐛​h​(z)=0D^{\bf b}h(z)=0 iff the holomorphic part of the Laurent polynomial z−𝐛​h​(z)z^{-\bf b}h(z) is zero.

Now we fix a P⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[z]P(z)\in\mathbb{C}[z] and set f⁡(z):=z−𝐚​P​(z)f(z)\!:=z^{-\bf a}P(z). With the observation above, it is easy to see that, P⁡(z)P(z) is D𝐚D^{\bf a}-nilpotent iff the holomorphic parts of the Laurent polynomials fm​(z)f^{m}(z) (m≥1)(m\geq 1) are all zero; and VC holds for Λ\Lambda and P⁡(z)P(z) iff the holomorphic part of P⁡(z)​fm​(z)P(z)f^{m}(z) is zero when m>>0m>>0. Therefore, VC for D𝐚D^{\bf a} can be restated as follows:

Re-Stated VC for Λ=D𝐚\Lambda=D^{\bf a}: Let P⁡(z)∈𝒜nP(z)\in{\mathcal{A}}_{n} and f⁡(z)f(z) as above. Suppose that, for any m≥1m\geq 1, the holomorphic part of the Laurent polynomial fm​(z)f^{m}(z) is zero, then the holomorphic part of P⁡(z)​fm​(z)P(z)f^{m}(z) equals to zero when m>>0m>>0.

Note that the re-stated VC above is very similar to the following non-trivial theorem which was first conjectured by O. Mathieu [Ma] and later proved by J. Duistermaat and W. van der Kallen [DK].

Theorem 3.20.

Let ff and gg be Laurent polynomials in zz. Assume that, for any m≥1m\geq 1, the constant term of fmf^{m} is zero. Then the constant term g​fmgf^{m} equals to zero when m>>0m>>0.

Note that, Mathieu’s conjecture [Ma] is a conjecture on all real compact Lie groups GG, which is also mainly motivated by JC. The theorem above is the special case of Mathieu’s conjecture when GG the nn-dimensional real torus. For other compact real Lie groups, Mathieu’s conjecture seems to be still wide open.

Motivated by Theorem 3.20, the above re-stated VC for Λ=D𝐚\Lambda=D^{\bf a} and also the result on VC in Theorem 3.16, we would like to propose the following conjecture on Laurent polynomials.

Conjecture 3.21.

Let ff and gg be Laurent polynomials in zz. Assume that, for any m≥1m\geq 1, the holomorphic part of fmf^{m} is zero. Then the holomorphic part g​fmgf^{m} equals to zero when m>>0m>>0.

Note that, a positive answer to the conjecture above will imply VC for Λ=D𝐚\Lambda=D^{\bf a} (𝐚∈ℕn)({\bf a}\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}) by simply choosing g⁡(z)g(z) to be P⁡(z)P(z).

Finally let us to point out that, it is well-known that JC does not hold over fields of finite characteristic (see [BCW], for example), but, by Proposition 5.35.3 in [Z3], the situation for VC over fields of finite characteristic is dramatically different even though it is equivalent to JC over the complex field ℂ\mathbb{C}.

Proposition 3.22.

Let kk be a field of c​h​a​r.p>0char.\,p>0 and Λ\Lambda any differential operator of k⁡[z]k[z]. Let f∈k⁡[[z]]f\in k[[z]]. Assume that, for any 1≤m≤p−11\leq m\leq p-1, there exists Nm>0N_{m}>0 such that ΛNm​fm=0\Lambda^{N_{m}}f^{m}=0. Then, Λm​fm+1=0\Lambda^{m}f^{m+1}=0 when m>>0m>>0.

From the proposition above, we immediately have the following corollary.

Corollary 3.23.

Let kk be a field of c​h​a​r.p>0char.\,p>0. Then

(a)(a) VC holds for any differential operator Λ\Lambda of k⁡[z]k[z].

(b)(b) If Λ\Lambda strictly decreases the degree of polynomials. Then, for any polynomial f∈k⁡[z]f\in k[z] ((not necessarily Λ\Lambda-nilpotent)), we have Λm​fm+1=0\Lambda^{m}f^{m+1}=0 when m>>0m>>0.

4. A Remark on Λ\Lambda-Nilpotent Polynomials and Classical Orthogonal Polynomials

In this section, we first in subsection 4.1 consider the “formal” connection between Λ\Lambda-nilpotent polynomials or formal power series and classical orthogonal polynomials, which has been discussed in Section 1 (see page 1). We then in subsection 4.2 transform the isotropic properties of homogeneous HN polynomials proved in [Z2] to isotropic properties of homogeneous ΔA\Delta_{A}-nilpotent (A∈S​G​L​(n,ℂ))(A\in SGL(n,\mathbb{C})) polynomials (see Theorem 4.10 and Corollary 4.11). Note that, as pointed in Section 1, the isotropic results in subsection 4.2 can be understood as some natural consequences of the connection of Λ\Lambda-nilpotent polynomials and classical orthogonal polynomials discussed in subsection 4.1.

4.1. Some Classical Orthogonal Polynomials

First, let us recall the definition of classical orthogonal polynomials. Note that, to be consistent with the tradition for orthogonal polynomials, we will in this subsection use x=(x1,x2,…,xn)x=(x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{n}) instead of z=(z1,z2,…,zn)z=(z_{1},z_{2},\dots,z_{n}) to denote free commutative variables.

Definition 4.1.

Let BB be an open set of ℝn{\mathbb{R}}^{n} and w⁡(x)w(x) a real valued function defined over BB such that w⁡(x)≥0w(x)\geq 0 for any x∈Bx\in B and 0<∫Bw⁡(x)​𝑑x<∞0<\int_{B}w(x)dx<\infty. A sequence of polynomials {f𝐦​(x)|𝐦∈ℕn}\{f_{\bf m}(x)\,|\,{\bf m}\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}\} is said to be orthogonal over BB if
(1)(1) deg⁡f𝐦=|𝐦|\deg f_{\bf m}=|{\bf m}| for any 𝐦∈ℕn{\bf m}\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}.
(2)(2) ∫Bf𝐦​(x)​f𝐤​(x)​w​(x)​𝑑x=0\int_{B}f_{\bf m}(x)f_{\bf k}(x)w(x)\,dx=0 for any 𝐦≠𝐤∈ℕn{\bf m}\neq{\bf k}\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}.

The function w⁡(x)w(x) is called the weight function. When the open set B⊂ℝnB\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{n} and w⁡(x)w(x) are clear in the context, we simply call the polynomials f𝐦​(x)f_{\bf m}(x) (𝐦∈ℕn)({\bf m}\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}) in the definition above orthogonal polynomials. If the orthogonal polynomials f𝐦​(x)f_{\bf m}(x) (𝐦∈ℕn)({\bf m}\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}) also satisfy ∫Bf𝐦2​(x)​w​(x)​𝑑x=1\int_{B}f_{\bf m}^{2}(x)w(x)dx=1 for any 𝐦∈ℕn{\bf m}\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}, we call f𝐦​(x)f_{\bf m}(x) (𝐦∈ℕn)({\bf m}\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}) orthonormal polynomials. Note that, in the one dimensional case w⁡(x)w(x) determines orthogonal polynomials over BB up to multiplicative constants, i.e. if fm​(x)f_{m}(x) (m≥0)(m\geq 0) are orthogonal polynomials as in Definition 4.1, then, for any am∈ℝ×a_{m}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{\times} (m≥0)(m\geq 0), am​fma_{m}f_{m} (m≥0)(m\geq 0) are also orthogonal over BB with respect to the weight function w⁡(x)w(x).

The most natural way to construct orthogonal or orthonormal sequences is: first to list all monomials in an order such that the degrees of monomials are non-decreasing; and then to apply Gram-Schmidt procedure to orthogonalize or orthonormalize the sequence of monomials. But, surprisingly, most of classical orthogonal polynomials can also be obtained by the so-called Rodrigues’ formulas.

We first consider orthogonal polynomials in one variable.

Rodrigues’ formula: Let fm​(x)f_{m}(x) (m≥0)(m\geq 0) be the orthogonal polynomials as in Definition 4.1. Then, there exist a function g⁡(x)g(x) defined over BB and non-zero constants cm∈ℝc_{m}\in{\mathbb{R}} (m≥0)(m\geq 0) such that

(4.1) fm​(x)=cm​w​(x)−1​dmd​xm​(w⁡(x)​gm​(x)).\displaystyle f_{m}(x)=c_{m}w(x)^{-1}\frac{d^{m}}{dx^{m}}(w(x)g^{m}(x)).

Let P⁡(x):=g⁡(x)P(x)\!:=g(x) and Λ:=w​(x)−1​(dd​x)​w​(x)\Lambda\!:=w(x)^{-1}\left(\frac{d}{dx}\right)w(x), where, throughout this paper any polynomial or function appearing in a (differential) operator always means the multiplication operator by the polynomial or function itself. Then, by Rodrigues’ formula above, we see that the orthogonal polynomials {fm​(x)|m≥0}\{f_{m}(x)\,|\,m\geq 0\} have the form

(4.2) fm​(x)=cm​Λm​Pm​(x),\displaystyle f_{m}(x)=c_{m}\Lambda^{m}P^{m}(x),

for any m≥0m\geq 0.

In other words, all orthogonal polynomials in one variable, up to multiplicative constants, has the form {Λm​Pm|m≥0}\{\Lambda^{m}P^{m}\,|\,m\geq 0\} for a single differential operator Λ\Lambda and a single function P⁡(x)P(x).

Next we consider some of the most well-known classical orthonormal polynomials in one variable. For more details on these orthogonal polynomials, see [Sz], [AS], [DX].

Example 4.2.

(Hermite Polynomials)

(a)(a) B=ℝB={\mathbb{R}} and the weight function w⁡(x)=e−x2w(x)=e^{-x^{2}}.

(b)(b) Rodrigues’ formula:

Hm​(x)=(−1)m​ex2​(dd​x)m​e−x2.\displaystyle H_{m}(x)=(-1)^{m}e^{x^{2}}(\frac{d}{dx})^{m}e^{-x^{2}}.

(c)(c) Differential operator Λ\Lambda and polynomial P⁡(x)P(x):

{Λ=ex2​(dd​x)​e−x2=dd​x−2​x,P⁡(x)=1,\displaystyle\begin{cases}\Lambda=e^{x^{2}}(\frac{d}{dx})e^{-x^{2}}=\frac{d}{dx}-2x,\\ P(x)=1,\end{cases}

(d)(d) Hermite polynomials in terms of Λ\Lambda and P⁡(x)P(x):

Hm​(x)=(−1)m​Λm​Pm​(x).\displaystyle H_{m}(x)=(-1)^{m}\,\Lambda^{m}P^{m}(x).
Example 4.3.

(Laguerre Polynomials)

(a)(a) B=ℝ+B={\mathbb{R}}^{+} and w⁡(x)=xα​e−xw(x)=x^{\alpha}e^{-x} (α>−1)(\alpha>-1).

(b)(b) Rodrigues’ formula:

Lmα​(x)=1m!​x−α​ex​(dd​x)m​(xm+α​e−x).\displaystyle L_{m}^{\alpha}(x)=\frac{1}{m!}x^{-\alpha}e^{x}(\frac{d}{dx})^{m}(x^{m+\alpha}e^{-x}).

(c)(c) Differential operator Λ\Lambda and polynomial P⁡(x)P(x):

{Λα=x−α​ex​(dd​x)​(e−x​xα)=dd​x+(α​x−1−1),P⁡(x)=x,\displaystyle\begin{cases}\Lambda_{\alpha}=x^{-\alpha}e^{x}(\frac{d}{dx})(e^{-x}x^{\alpha})=\frac{d}{dx}+(\alpha x^{-1}-1),\\ P(x)=x,\end{cases}

(d)(d) Laguerre polynomials in terms of Λ\Lambda and P⁡(x)P(x):

Lm​(x)=1m!​Λm​Pm​(x).\displaystyle L_{m}(x)=\frac{1}{m!}\,\Lambda^{m}P^{m}(x).
Example 4.4.

(Jacobi Polynomials)

(a)(a) B=(−1,1)B=(-1,1) and w⁡(x)=(1−x)α​(1+x)βw(x)=(1-x)^{\alpha}(1+x)^{\beta}, where α,β>−1\alpha,\beta>-1.

(b)(b) Rodrigues’ formula:

Pmα,β​(x)=(−1)m2m​m!​(1−x)−α​(1+x)−β​(dd​x)m​(1−x)α+m​(1+x)β+m.\displaystyle P_{m}^{\alpha,\beta}(x)=\frac{(-1)^{m}}{2^{m}m!}(1-x)^{-\alpha}(1+x)^{-\beta}(\frac{d}{dx})^{m}(1-x)^{\alpha+m}(1+x)^{\beta+m}.

(c)(c) Differential operator Λ\Lambda and polynomial P⁡(x)P(x):

Λ\displaystyle\Lambda =(1−x)−α​(1+x)−β​(dd​x)​(1−x)α​(1+x)β\displaystyle=(1-x)^{-\alpha}(1+x)^{-\beta}(\frac{d}{dx})(1-x)^{\alpha}(1+x)^{\beta}
=dd​x−α​(1−x)−1+β​(1+x)−1,\displaystyle=\frac{d}{dx}-\alpha(1-x)^{-1}+\beta(1+x)^{-1},

and

P⁡(x)=1−x2.\displaystyle P(x)=1-x^{2}.

(d)(d) Laguerre polynomials in terms of Λ\Lambda and P⁡(x)P(x):

Pmα,β​(x)=(−1)m2m​m!​Λm​Pm​(x).\displaystyle P^{\alpha,\beta}_{m}(x)=\frac{(-1)^{m}}{2^{m}m!}\,\Lambda^{m}P^{m}(x).

A very important special family of Jacobi polynomials are the Gegenbauer polynomials which are obtained by setting α=β=λ−1/2\alpha=\beta=\lambda-1/2 for some λ>−1/2\lambda>-1/2. Gegenbauer polynomials are also called ultraspherical polynomials in the literature.

Example 4.5.

(Gegenbauer Polynomials)

(a)(a) B=(−1,1)B=(-1,1) and w⁡(x)=(1−x2)λ−1/2w(x)=(1-x^{2})^{\lambda-1/2}, where λ>−1/2\lambda>-1/2.

(b)(b) Rodrigues’ formula:

Pmλ​(x)=(−1)m2m​(λ+1/2)m​(1−x2)1/2−λ​(dd​x)m​(1−x2)m+λ−1/2.\displaystyle P_{m}^{\lambda}(x)=\frac{(-1)^{m}}{2^{m}(\lambda+1/2)_{m}}(1-x^{2})^{1/2-\lambda}(\frac{d}{dx})^{m}(1-x^{2})^{m+\lambda-1/2}.

where, for any c∈ℝc\in{\mathbb{R}} and k∈ℕk\in{\mathbb{N}}, (c)k=c(c+1)⋯(c+k−1)(c)_{k}=c(c+1)\cdots(c+k-1).

(c)(c) Differential operator Λ\Lambda and polynomial P⁡(x)P(x):

(4.3) Λ\displaystyle\Lambda =(1−x2)1/2−λ​(dd​x)​(1−x2)λ−1/2\displaystyle=(1-x^{2})^{1/2-\lambda}(\frac{d}{dx})(1-x^{2})^{\lambda-1/2}
=dd​x−(2​λ−1)​x(1−x2),\displaystyle=\frac{d}{dx}-\frac{(2\lambda-1)\,x}{(1-x^{2})},

and

P⁡(x)=1−x2.\displaystyle P(x)=1-x^{2}.

(d)(d) Laguerre polynomials in terms of Λ\Lambda and P⁡(x)P(x):

Pmλ​(x)=(−1)m2m​(λ+1/2)m​Λm​Pm​(x).\displaystyle P_{m}^{\lambda}(x)=\frac{(-1)^{m}}{2^{m}(\lambda+1/2)_{m}}\,\Lambda^{m}P^{m}(x).

Note that, for the special cases with λ=0,1,1/2\lambda=0,1,1/2, the Gegenbauer Polynomials Pmλ​(x)P_{m}^{\lambda}(x) are called the Chebyshev polynomial of the first kind, the second kind and Legendre polynomials, respectively. Hence all these classical orthogonal polynomials also have the form of Λm​Pm\Lambda^{m}P^{m} (m≥0)(m\geq 0) up to some scalar multiple constants cmc_{m} with P⁡(x)=1−x2P(x)=1-x^{2} and the corresponding special forms of the differential operator Λ\Lambda in Eq. (4.3)(\ref{Ge-OP-e1}).

Remark 4.6.

Actually, the Gegenbauer polynomials are more closely and directly related with VC in some different ways. See [Z4] for more discussions on connections of the Gegenbauer polynomials with VC.

Next, we consider some classical orthogonal polynomials in several variables. We will see that they can also be obtained from certain sequences of the form {Λm​Pm|m≥0}\{\Lambda^{m}P^{m}\,|\,m\geq 0\} in a slightly modified way. One remark is that, unlike the one-variable case, orthogonal polynomials in several variables up to multiplicative constants are not uniquely determined by weight functions.

The first family of classical orthogonal polynomials in several variables can be constructed by taking Cartesian products of orthogonal polynomials in one variable as follows.

Suppose {fm|m≥0}\{f_{m}\,|\,m\geq 0\} is a sequence of orthogonal polynomials in one variable, say as given in Definition 4.1. We fix any n≥2n\geq 2 and set

(4.4) W⁡(x):=\displaystyle W(x)\!:= ∏i=1nw⁡(xi),\displaystyle\prod_{i=1}^{n}w(x_{i}),
(4.5) f𝐦​(x):=\displaystyle f_{\bf m}(x)\!:= ∏i=1nfmi​(xi),\displaystyle\prod_{i=1}^{n}f_{m_{i}}(x_{i}),

for any x∈B×nx\in B^{\times n} and 𝐦∈ℕn{\bf m}\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}.

Then it is easy to see that the sequence {f𝐦​(x)|𝐦∈ℕn}\{f_{\bf m}(x)\,|\,{\bf m}\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}\} are orthogonal polynomials over B×nB^{\times n} with respect to the weight function W⁡(x)W(x) defined above.

Note that, by applying the construction above to the classical one-variable orthogonal polynomials discussed in the previous examples, one gets the classical multiple Hermite Polynomials, multiple Laguerre polynomials, multiple Jacobi polynomials and multiple Gegenbauer polynomials, respectively.

To see that the multi-variable orthogonal polynomials constructed above can be obtained from a sequence of the form {Λm​Pm​(x)|m≥0}\{\Lambda^{m}P^{m}(x)\,|\,m\geq 0\}, we suppose fmf_{m} (m≥0)(m\geq 0) have Rodrigues’ formula Eq. (4.1)(\ref{Rodrigues}). Let s=(s1,…,sn)s=(s_{1},\dots,s_{n}) be nn central formal parameters and set

(4.6) Λs:=\displaystyle\Lambda_{s}\!:= W​(x)−1​(∑i=1nsi​∂∂xi)​W​(x),\displaystyle W(x)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}s_{i}\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{i}}\right)W(x),
(4.7) P⁡(x):=\displaystyle P(x)\!:= ∏i=1ng⁡(xi).\displaystyle\prod_{i=1}^{n}g(x_{i}).

Let V𝐦​(x)V_{\bf m}(x) (𝐦∈ℕn)({\bf m}\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}) be the coefficient of s𝐦s^{\bf m} in Λs|𝐦|​P|𝐦|​(x)\Lambda_{s}^{|\bf m|}P^{|\bf m|}(x). Then, from Eqs. (4.1)(\ref{Rodrigues}), (4.4)(\ref{Wx})–(4.7)(\ref{Px}), it is easy to check that, for any 𝐦∈ℕn{\bf m}\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}, we have

(4.8) f𝐦​(x)=c𝐦​𝐦!|𝐦|!​V𝐦​(x),\displaystyle f_{\bf m}(x)=c_{\bf m}\frac{{\bf m}!}{|\bf m|!}\,V_{\bf m}(x),

where c𝐦=∏i=1ncmic_{\bf m}=\prod_{i=1}^{n}c_{m_{i}}.

Therefore, we see that any multi-variable orthogonal polynomials constructed as above from Cartesian products of one-variable orthogonal polynomials can also be obtained from a single differential operator Λs\Lambda_{s} and a single function P⁡(x)P(x) via the sequence {Λsm​Pm|m≥0}\{\Lambda_{s}^{m}P^{m}\,|\,m\geq 0\}.

Remark 4.7.

Note that, one can also take Cartesian products of different kinds of one-variable orthogonal polynomials to create more orthogonal polynomials in several variables. By a similar argument as above, we see that all these multi-variable orthogonal polynomials can also be obtained similarly from a single sequence {Λsm​Pm|m≥0}\{\Lambda_{s}^{m}P^{m}\,|\,m\geq 0\}.

Next, we consider the following two examples of classical multi-variable orthogonal polynomials which are not Cartesian products of one-variable orthogonal polynomials.

Example 4.8.

(Classical Orthogonal Polynomials over Unit Balls)

(a)(a) Choose BB to be the open unit ball 𝔹n{\mathbb{B}}^{n} of ℝn{\mathbb{R}}^{n} and the weight function

Wμ​(x)=(1−‖x‖2)μ−1/2,\displaystyle W_{\mu}(x)=(1-||x||^{2})^{\mu-1/2},

where ‖x‖=∑i=1nxi2||x||=\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}^{2} and μ>1/2\mu>1/2.

(b)(b) Rodrigues’ formula: For any 𝐦∈ℕn{\bf m}\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}, set

U𝐦​(x):=(−1)𝐦​(2​μ)|𝐦|2|𝐦|​𝐦!​(μ+1/2)|𝐦|​∂|𝐦|∂x1m1⋯∂xnmn​(1−‖x‖2)|𝐦|+μ−𝟏/𝟐.\displaystyle U_{\bf m}(x)\!:=\frac{(-1)^{\bf m}(2\mu)_{|\bf m|}}{2^{|\bf m|}{\bf m}!(\mu+1/2)_{|\bf m|}}\frac{\partial^{|\bf m|}}{\partial x_{1}^{m_{1}}\cdots\partial x_{n}^{m_{n}}}(1-||x||^{2})^{|\bf m|+\mu-1/2}.

Then, by Proposition 2.2.52.2.5 in [DX], {U𝐦​(x)|𝐦∈ℕn}\{U_{\bf m}(x)\,|\,{\bf m}\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}\} are orthonormal over 𝔹n{\mathbb{B}}^{n} with respect to the weight function Wμ​(x)W_{\mu}(x).

(c)(c) Differential operator Λs\Lambda_{s} and polynomial P⁡(x)P(x): Let s=(s1,…,sn)s=(s_{1},\dots,s_{n}) be nn central formal parameters and set

Λs:=\displaystyle\Lambda_{s}\!:= Wμ​(x)−1​(∑i=1nsi​∂∂xi)​Wμ​(x),\displaystyle W_{\mu}(x)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}s_{i}\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{i}}\right)W_{\mu}(x),
P⁡(x):=\displaystyle P(x)\!:= 1−‖x‖2.\displaystyle 1-||x||^{2}.

Let V𝐦​(x)V_{\bf m}(x) (𝐦∈ℕn)({\bf m}\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}) be the coefficient of s𝐦s^{\bf m} in Λs|𝐦|​P|𝐦|​(x)\Lambda_{s}^{|\bf m|}P^{|\bf m|}(x). Then from the Rodrigues type formula above, we have, for any 𝐦∈ℕn{\bf m}\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n},

U𝐦​(x)=(−1)|𝐦|​(2​μ)|𝐦|2|𝐦|​|𝐦|!​(μ+1/2)|𝐦|​V𝐦​(x).\displaystyle U_{\bf m}(x)=\frac{(-1)^{|\bf m|}(2\mu)_{|\bf m|}}{2^{|{\bf m}|}{|\bf m|}!(\mu+1/2)_{|\bf m|}}\,V_{\bf m}(x).

Therefore, the classical orthonormal polynomials {U𝐦​(x)|𝐦∈ℕn}\{U_{\bf m}(x)\,|\,{\bf m}\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}\} over 𝔹n{\mathbb{B}}^{n} can be obtained from a single differential operator Λs\Lambda_{s} and P⁡(x)P(x) via the sequence {Λsm​Pm|m≥0}\{\Lambda_{s}^{m}P^{m}\,|\,m\geq 0\}.

Example 4.9.

(Classical Orthogonal Polynomials over Simplices)

(a)(a) Choose BB to be the simplex

Tn={x∈ℝn|∑i=1nxi​<1;x1,…,xn>​0}\displaystyle T^{n}=\{x\in{\mathbb{R}}^{n}\,|\,\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}<1;\,\,x_{1},...,x_{n}>0\}

in ℝn{\mathbb{R}}^{n} and the weight function

(4.9) Wκ(x)=x1κ1⋯xnκn(1−|x|1)κn+1−1/2,\displaystyle W_{\kappa}(x)=x_{1}^{\kappa_{1}}\cdots x_{n}^{\kappa_{n}}(1-|x|_{1})^{\kappa_{n+1}-1/2},

where κi>−1/2\kappa_{i}>-1/2 (1≤i≤n+1)(1\leq i\leq n+1) and |x|1=∑i=1nxi|x|_{1}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}.

U𝐦​(x):=Wκ​(x)−1​∂|𝐦|∂x1m1⋯∂xnmn​(Wκ​(x)​(1−|x|1)|𝐦|).\displaystyle U_{\bf m}(x)\!:=W_{\kappa}(x)^{-1}\frac{\partial^{|\bf m|}}{\partial x_{1}^{m_{1}}\cdots\partial x_{n}^{m_{n}}}\left(W_{\kappa}(x)(1-|x|_{1})^{|\bf m|}\right).

Then, {U𝐦​(x)|𝐦∈ℕn}\{U_{\bf m}(x)\,|\,{\bf m}\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}\} are orthonormal over TnT^{n} with respect to the weight function Wκ​(x)W_{\kappa}(x). See Section 2.3.32.3.3 of [DX] for a proof of this claim.

(c)(c) Differential operator Λ\Lambda and polynomial P⁡(x)P(x): Let s=(s1,…,sn)s=(s_{1},\dots,s_{n}) be nn central formal parameters and set

Λs:=\displaystyle\Lambda_{s}\!:= Wκ​(x)−1​(∑i=1nsi​∂∂xi)​Wκ​(x),\displaystyle W_{\kappa}(x)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}s_{i}\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{i}}\right)W_{\kappa}(x),
P⁡(x):=\displaystyle P(x)\!:= 1−|x|1.\displaystyle 1-|x|_{1}.

Let V𝐦​(x)V_{\bf m}(x) (𝐦∈ℕn)({\bf m}\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}) be the coefficient of s𝐦s^{\bf m} in Λs|𝐦|​P|𝐦|​(x)\Lambda_{s}^{|\bf m|}P^{|\bf m|}(x). Then from the Rodrigues type formula in (b)(b), we have, for any 𝐦∈ℕn{\bf m}\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n},

U𝐦​(x)=𝐦!|𝐦|!​V𝐦​(x).\displaystyle U_{\bf m}(x)=\frac{{\bf m}!}{|\bf m|!}\,V_{\bf m}(x).

Therefore, the classical orthonormal polynomials {U𝐦​(x)|𝐦∈ℕn}\{U_{\bf m}(x)\,|\,{\bf m}\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}\} over TnT^{n} can be obtained from a single differential operator Λs\Lambda_{s} and a function P⁡(x)P(x) via the sequence {Λsm​Pm|m≥0}\{\Lambda_{s}^{m}P^{m}\,|\,m\geq 0\}.

4.2. The Isotropic Property of ΔA\Delta_{A}-Nilpotent Polynomials

As discussed in Section 1, the “formal” connection of Λ\Lambda-nilpotent polynomials with classical orthogonal polynomials predicts that Λ\Lambda-nilpotent polynomials should be isotropic with respect to a certain ℂ\mathbb{C}-bilinear form of 𝒜n{\mathcal{A}}_{n}. In this subsection, we show that, for differential operators Λ=ΔA\Lambda=\Delta_{A} (A∈S​G​L​(n,ℂ))(A\in SGL(n,\mathbb{C})), this is indeed the case for any homogeneous Λ\Lambda-nilpotent polynomials (see Theorem 4.10 and Corollaries 4.11, 4.12).

We fix any n≥1n\geq 1 and let zz and DD denote the n-tuples (z1,…,zn)(z_{1},\dots,z_{n}) and (D1,D2,…,Dn)(D_{1},D_{2},\dots,D_{n}), respectively. Let A∈S​G​L​(n,ℂ)A\in SGL(n,\mathbb{C}) and define the ℂ\mathbb{C}-bilinear map

(4.10) {⋅,⋅}A:𝒜n×𝒜n\displaystyle\{\cdot,\cdot\}_{A}:{\mathcal{A}}_{n}\times{\mathcal{A}}_{n} →𝒜n\displaystyle\to\quad{\mathcal{A}}_{n}
(f,g)\displaystyle(f,\,g)\quad →f⁡(A​D)​g​(z),\displaystyle\to f(AD)g(z),

Furthermore, we also define a ℂ\mathbb{C}-bilinear form

(4.11) (⋅,⋅)A:𝒜n×𝒜n\displaystyle(\cdot,\cdot)_{A}:{\mathcal{A}}_{n}\times{\mathcal{A}}_{n} →ℂ\displaystyle\to\quad\mathbb{C}
(f,g)\displaystyle(f,\,g)\quad →{f,g}A|z=0,\displaystyle\to\{f,g\}_{{}_{A}}|_{z=0},

It is straightforward to check that the ℂ\mathbb{C}-bilinear form defined above is symmetric and its restriction on the subspace of homogeneous polynomials of any fixed degree is non-singular. Note also that, for any homogeneous polynomials f,g∈𝒜nf,g\in{\mathcal{A}}_{n} of the same degree, we have {f,g}A=(f,g)A\{f,g\}_{A}=(f,g)_{A}.

The main result of this subsection is the following theorem.

Theorem 4.10.

Let A∈S​G​L​(n,ℂ)A\in SGL(n,\mathbb{C}) and P⁡(z)∈𝒜nP(z)\in{\mathcal{A}}_{n} a homogeneous ΔA\Delta_{A}-nilpotent polynomial of degree d≥3d\geq 3. Let ℐ⁡(P){\mathcal{I}}(P) be the ideal of 𝒜n{\mathcal{A}}_{n} generated by σA−1​(z):=zτ​A−1​z\sigma_{A^{-1}}(z)\!:=z^{\tau}A^{-1}z and ∂P∂zi\frac{\partial P}{\partial z_{i}} (1≤i≤n)(1\leq i\leq n). Then, for any f⁡(z)∈ℐ⁡(P)f(z)\in{\mathcal{I}}(P) and m≥0m\geq 0, we have

(4.12) {f,ΔAm​Pm+1}A=f⁡(A​D)​ΔAm​Pm+1=0.\displaystyle\{f,\Delta_{A}^{m}P^{m+1}\}_{A}=f(AD)\,\Delta_{A}^{m}P^{m+1}=0.

Note that, by Theorem 6.36.3 in [Z2], we know that the theorem does hold when A=InA=I_{n} and ΔA=Δn\Delta_{A}=\Delta_{n}.

Proof:  Note first that, elements of 𝒜n{\mathcal{A}}_{n} satisfying Eq. (4.12)(\ref{A-Isotropic-e}) do form an ideal. Therefore, it will be enough to show σA−1​(z)\sigma_{A^{-1}}(z) and ∂P∂zi\frac{\partial P}{\partial z_{i}} (1≤i≤n)(1\leq i\leq n) satisfy Eq. (4.12)(\ref{A-Isotropic-e}). But Eq. (4.12)(\ref{A-Isotropic-e}) for σA−1​(z)\sigma_{A^{-1}}(z) simply follows the facts that σA−1​(A​z)=zτ​A​z\sigma_{A^{-1}}(Az)=z^{\tau}Az and σA−1​(A​D)=ΔA\sigma_{A^{-1}}(AD)=\Delta_{A}.

Secondly, by Lemma 2.2, we can write A=U​UτA=UU^{\tau} for some U=(ui​j)∈G​L​(n,ℂ)U=(u_{ij})\in GL(n,\mathbb{C}). Then, by Eq. (2.7)(\ref{L2.1-e2}), we have ΨU​(Δn)=ΔA\Psi_{U}(\Delta_{n})=\Delta_{A} or ΨU−1​(ΔA)=Δn\Psi_{U}^{-1}(\Delta_{A})=\Delta_{n}. Let P~​(z):=ΦU−1​(P)=P⁡(U​z)\widetilde{P}(z)\!:=\Phi_{U}^{-1}(P)=P(Uz). Then by Lemma 2.5, (a)(a), P~\widetilde{P} is a homogeneous Δn\Delta_{n}-nilpotent polynomial, and by Eq. (2.6)(\ref{L2.1-e1}), we also have

(4.13) ΦU−1​(ΔAm​Pm+1)=Δnm​P~m+1.\displaystyle\Phi_{U}^{-1}(\Delta_{A}^{m}P^{m+1})=\Delta_{n}^{m}\widetilde{P}^{m+1}.

By Theorem 6.36.3 in [Z2], for any 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n and m≥0m\geq 0, we have,

∂P~∂zi​(D)​(Δnm​P~m+1)=0\displaystyle\frac{\partial\widetilde{P}}{\partial z_{i}}(D)\left(\Delta_{n}^{m}\widetilde{P}^{m+1}\right)=0

Since

∂P~∂zi​(z)=∑k=1nuk​i​∂P∂zk​(U​z),\displaystyle\frac{\partial\widetilde{P}}{\partial z_{i}}(z)=\sum_{k=1}^{n}u_{ki}\frac{\partial P}{\partial z_{k}}(Uz),

we further have,

∑k=1nuk​i​∂P∂zk​(U​D)​(Δnm​P~m+1)=0.\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{n}u_{ki}\frac{\partial P}{\partial z_{k}}(UD)\left(\Delta_{n}^{m}\widetilde{P}^{m+1}\right)=0.

Since UU is invertible, for any 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n, we have

(4.14) ∂P∂zi​(U​D)​(Δnm​P~m+1)=0.\displaystyle\frac{\partial P}{\partial z_{i}}(UD)\left(\Delta_{n}^{m}\widetilde{P}^{m+1}\right)=0.

Combining the equation above with Eq. (4.13)(\ref{A-Isotropic-pe1}), we get

∂P∂zi​(U​D)​ΦU−1​(ΔAm​Pm+1)=0.\displaystyle\frac{\partial P}{\partial z_{i}}(UD)\Phi_{U}^{-1}\left(\Delta_{A}^{m}P^{m+1}\right)=0.
ΦU−1​(ΦU​∂P∂zi​(U​D)​ΦU−1)​(ΔAm​Pm+1)=0.\displaystyle\Phi_{U}^{-1}(\Phi_{U}\frac{\partial P}{\partial z_{i}}(UD)\Phi_{U}^{-1})\left(\Delta_{A}^{m}P^{m+1}\right)=0.
(4.15) (ΦU​∂P∂zi​(U​D)​ΦU−1)​(ΔAm​Pm+1)=0.\displaystyle(\Phi_{U}\frac{\partial P}{\partial z_{i}}(UD)\Phi_{U}^{-1})\left(\Delta_{A}^{m}P^{m+1}\right)=0.

By Lemma 2.1, (b)(b), Eq. (4.15)(\ref{A-Isotropic-pe3}) and the fact that A=U​UτA=UU^{\tau}, we get

∂P∂zi​(U​Uτ​D)​(ΔAm​Pm+1)=∂P∂zi​(A​D)​(ΔAm​Pm+1)=0,\displaystyle\frac{\partial P}{\partial z_{i}}(UU^{\tau}D)\left(\Delta_{A}^{m}P^{m+1}\right)=\frac{\partial P}{\partial z_{i}}(AD)\left(\Delta_{A}^{m}P^{m+1}\right)=0,

which is Eq. (4.12)(\ref{A-Isotropic-e}) for ∂P∂zi\frac{\partial P}{\partial z_{i}} (1≤i≤n)(1\leq i\leq n).   □\Box

Corollary 4.11.

Let AA be as in Theorem 4.10 and P⁡(z)P(z) be a homogeneous ΔA\Delta_{A}-nilpotent polynomial of degree d≥3d\geq 3. Then, for any m≥1m\geq 1, ΔAm​Pm+1\Delta_{A}^{m}P^{m+1} is isotropic with respect to the ℂ\mathbb{C}-bilinear form (⋅,⋅)A(\cdot,\cdot)_{A}, i.e.

(4.16) (ΔAm​Pm+1,ΔAm​Pm+1)A=0.\displaystyle(\Delta_{A}^{m}P^{m+1},\Delta_{A}^{m}P^{m+1})_{A}=0.

In particular, we have (P,P)A=0(P,P)_{A}=0.

Proof:  By the definition Eq. (4.11)(\ref{A-Bi-form}) of the ℂ\mathbb{C}-bilinear form (⋅,⋅)A(\cdot,\cdot)_{A} and Theorem 4.10, it will be enough to show that PP and ΔAm​Pm+1\Delta_{A}^{m}P^{m+1} (m≥1)(m\geq 1) belong to the ideal generated by the polynomials ∂P∂zi\frac{\partial P}{\partial z_{i}} (1≤i≤n)(1\leq i\leq n) (here we do not need to consider the polynomial σA−1​(z)\sigma_{A^{-1}}(z)). But this statement has been proved in the proof of Corollary 6.76.7 in [Z2]. So we refer the reader to [Z2] for a proof of the statement above.   □\Box

Theorem 4.10 and Corollary 4.11 do not hold for homogeneous HN polynomials P⁡(z)P(z) of degree d=2d=2. But, by applying similar arguments as in the proof of Theorem 4.10 above to Proposition 6.86.8 in [Z2], one can show that the following proposition holds.

Proposition 4.12.

Let AA be as in Theorem 4.10 and P⁡(z)P(z) a homogeneous ΔA\Delta_{A}-nilpotent polynomial of degree d=2d=2. Let 𝒥⁡(P){\mathcal{J}}(P) the ideal of ℂ⁡[z]\mathbb{C}[z] generated by P⁡(z)P(z) and σA−1​(z)\sigma_{A^{-1}}(z). Then, for any f⁡(z)∈𝒥⁡(P)f(z)\in{\mathcal{J}}(P) and m≥0m\geq 0, we have

(4.17) {f,ΔAm​Pm+1}A=f⁡(A​D)​ΔAm​Pm+1=0.\displaystyle\{f,\Delta_{A}^{m}P^{m+1}\}_{A}=f(AD)\,\Delta_{A}^{m}P^{m+1}=0.

In particular, we still have (P,P)A=0(P,P)_{A}=0.
